{"id": "26:115/q01", "question": "What does the restriction إِنْ ... إِلَّا convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:115/q01/p1", "position": "It confines Noah to the role of a clear warner, excluding compliance with the chiefs' wishes as part of his commission.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr calls this an additional restriction that limits the described subject to one quality. Alūsī reports a view that placing the pronoun after negation makes this and the preceding clause together answer the demand to expel believers; he notes a difficulty with that view. Sāmarrāʾī points to his earlier comparison of negation particles and cites parallel formulations of being only a clear warner, without stating a further conclusion here."}]}
{"id": "26:115/q02", "question": "How is أَنَا۠ read?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:115/q02/p1", "position": "The final alif can be shortened, producing ana rather than anā.", "reasons": "QIRAAT-ER names Qālūn and Ibn Kathīr as examples of the shortened reading. It says the difference changes cadence but not meaning; anā is the contrasted unshortened form."}]}
{"id": "26:115/q03", "question": "What role does Noah claim by calling himself نَذِيرٌۭ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:115/q03/p1", "position": "Noah is a messenger whose assigned task is to warn people plainly and call them to God; their response and standing are not his to control.", "reasons": "Muqātil and the Muqātil report in Wāḥidī say 'messenger'; Yaḥyā ibn Sallām and Elmalılı simply say 'clear warner.' Ṭabarī says Noah warns from his Lord, with no counsel concealed. Ṭabrisī mentions a call to obedience. Rāzī says the mission addresses rejecters and makes accepting followers near to Noah. Qurṭubī says Noah conveys God's message without favoring the rich. Bayḍāwī, Būrsawī, and Alūsī say the warning addresses accountable people regardless of rank; Bayḍāwī also offers the duty of warning with proof as an alternative account. Nasafī says sound proof leaves hearers responsible for their course; Abū Ḥayyān also mentions sound proof. Ibn Kathīr says believing followers belong with Noah regardless of status. Biqāʿī excludes probing inner states or imposing demands on followers. Alūsī's alternative says clear proof has already been delivered. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the role explains refusal of the chiefs' demand. Iṣlāḥī says Noah has discharged his duty and rejection is the rejecter's responsibility."}]}
{"id": "26:115/q04", "question": "What does Noah warn people about?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:115/q04/p1", "position": "He warns of the Fire and divine punishment for unbelief and sins, urging people away from what displeases God.", "reasons": "The Ibn ʿAbbās report in Ibn Abī Ḥātim specifies the Fire. The Ibn ʿAbbās report in Wāḥidī adds that Noah clarifies what brings people near to God. Ṭabarī specifies punishment for disbelief. Bayḍāwī names unbelief and sins; Alūsī describes deterrence from what God dislikes. Ṭabrisī says Noah calls people to obedience. Būrsawī stresses that this warning addresses both elite and poor accountable people."}]}
{"id": "26:115/q05", "question": "What does مُّبِينٌۭ add to the warning?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:115/q05/p1", "position": "The warning is made clear through explanation and proof, without obscurity or concealed counsel.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr derives mubīn from transitive abāna, 'to make clear or explain.' Ṭabarī says Noah made his warning plain and concealed no counsel, mentioning 2:168. Wāḥidī's Ibn ʿAbbās report says he clarifies what brings people near God. Nasafī and Abū Ḥayyān say sound proof distinguishes truth from falsehood; Abū Ḥayyān calls him a manifest warner. Bayḍāwī and Alūsī give clear proof as the alternative account of his duty. Biqāʿī says he explains without obscurity. Ṭabrisī calls him a clear warner inviting obedience."}]}
{"id": "26:115/q06", "question": "Where else does the clear-warner phrase occur?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:115/q06/p1", "position": "It recurs for Noah and is also used often for Muhammad.", "reasons": "The Study Quran lists Noah parallels at 7:184, 11:25, and 71:2, and Muhammad parallels at 15:89, 22:49, 29:50, 38:65, 38:70, 46:9, 51:50, and 67:26."}]}
{"id": "26:115/q07", "question": "What other role is نَذِيرٌۭ often paired with?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:115/q07/p1", "position": "A bearer of glad tidings, bashīr.", "reasons": "The Study Quran cites 4:165 for this frequent pairing."}]}
{"id": "26:115/q08", "question": "How does Noah's declared role answer the demand to expel believers?", "turns_on": "The notes offer different grounds for refusing expulsion: warning for all ranks, a duty already fulfilled by clear proof, God's authority over believers' hidden states, or the restrictive form of the reply. Bayḍāwī and Alūsī explicitly present the first two grounds as alternatives.", "positions": [{"id": "26:115/q08/p1", "position": "His warning addresses people regardless of status, and believers belong with him; he cannot exclude the poor to please the wealthy.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī says he refuses to expel those who believe and follow his message. Ṭabrisī rejects barring people from faith for being called low-status. Rāzī says acceptance brings a person near Noah and rejection makes one distant, so his mission supplies no grounds to expel believers. Qurṭubī says God did not send Noah to favor the rich and obedience makes even a poor person fortunate before God. Bayḍāwī's first explanation, Būrsawī, and Alūsī's first explanation say warning addresses all accountable people regardless of rank; expelling the poor to attract the wealthy contradicts the mission. Ibn Kathīr says obedient believers belong with Noah whatever their rank. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the role explains refusal of the chiefs' demand."}, {"id": "26:115/q08/p2", "position": "He is charged with delivering clear warning and proof, not satisfying listeners by expelling others; rejection remains each listener's responsibility.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī gives this as an alternative to the equal-address explanation. Nasafī says sound proof distinguishes truth from falsehood and leaves people responsible for their course. Alūsī gives the same alternative and says the proof has already been delivered. Iṣlāḥī says Noah will not abandon believers for acceptance, has discharged his duty as an open warner, and rejecters alone bear responsibility."}, {"id": "26:115/q08/p3", "position": "He is not charged with investigating believers' inward states or past deeds; their accounting belongs to God.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī says Noah is not tasked with probing inward states or imposing demands on followers. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says this statement explains why Noah will neither expel believers nor investigate their past to judge them, since God handles accounting."}, {"id": "26:115/q08/p4", "position": "The pronoun's place after negation restricts Noah to warning, so both preceding clauses reply by denying that he will follow the chiefs' wishes.", "reasons": "Alūsī reports this as one view of the two clauses, while noting a difficulty with it."}]}
{"id": "26:115/q09", "question": "Is Noah's similar exchange in Hūd the same occasion?", "turns_on": "Whether the accounts record one exchange with complementary details or two occasions; Ibn ʿĀshūr does not decide.", "positions": [{"id": "26:115/q09/p1", "position": "It may be the same exchange retold with complementary details.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr compares Hūd 11:29 and 11:31 and leaves this possibility open."}, {"id": "26:115/q09/p2", "position": "It may be a separate occasion.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr compares Hūd 11:29 and 11:31 and also leaves this possibility open."}]}
{"id": "26:115/q10", "question": "How does Noah's call fit the other prophet narratives in this sūra?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:115/q10/p1", "position": "Noah, Moses, and Abraham call to the same essential principles; their peoples' beliefs and responses are alike, so the three narrative groups convey the same message.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu compares the narratives and mentions 11:25 and 11:49."}]}
{"id": "26:116/q01", "question": "How forceful is the conditional threat?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:116/q01/p1", "position": "It is a sworn, firm and emphatic warning that they will carry out the threatened punishment.", "reasons": "Elmalılı notes that the people swear and say Noah will certainly be stoned unless he stops. Al-Tabatabaʾi says the emphatic assertion matches the warning's final and forceful character. Islahi infers that earlier threats of stoning had been ignored and that this emphatic wording now promises to carry them out."}]}
{"id": "26:116/q02", "question": "What does تَنتَهِ mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:116/q02/p1", "position": "To stop or desist, reaching a limit and going no further.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi explains intihāʾ as reaching a limit without passing the point where one has been forbidden, and nihāya as reaching a limit. Bursevi glosses intihāʾ as stopping or desisting."}]}
{"id": "26:116/q03", "question": "What did they demand Noah stop doing?", "turns_on": "Whether the conditional clause is described as Noah's refusal to stop his call or, in Ibn Kathir's note, as his stopping it.", "positions": [{"id": "26:116/q03/p1", "position": "Stop speaking to them and calling them to his message, including his criticism of their gods and religion.", "reasons": "Muqatil and al-Wahidi specify speaking and keeping quiet; Yahya ibn Sallam and al-Qurtubi add that the speech insulted or reviled their gods and criticized their religion. Al-Tabrisi says to cease what he said and called them to. Al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi refer to what he was saying; Bursevi and al-Tabatabaʾi specify preaching or warning. Study Quran reports the disbelievers' grievance as denigration of their gods and religion."}, {"id": "26:116/q03/p2", "position": "The threat is stated

 as applying if Noah stopped summoning them to his religion.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir's note gives this condition in these terms, reversing the condition stated in the other notes."}]}
{"id": "26:116/q04", "question": "Why did they address him as يَٰنُوحُ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:116/q04/p1", "position": "Calling him by name rather than by a respectful title shows rudeness and lack of manners.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī contrasts the bare name with a respectful title."}]}
{"id": "26:116/q05", "question": "What fate did they threaten by calling Noah one of ٱلْمَرْجُومِينَ?", "turns_on": "Whether rajm here is literal pelting, a general expression for killing, a metaphor for insults, or a designation of ill omen; the reports also differ for al-Ḍaḥḥāk.", "positions": [{"id": "26:116/q05/p1", "position": "He would be pelted with stones, commonly to death.", "reasons": "Qatāda is repeatedly reported to take rajm literally as stones (Yahya ibn Sallam, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Thaʿlabi, al-Māwardī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Tabrisi, al-Qurṭubī, al-Ālūsī). Al-Zajjāj also says rocks; al-Jishumī and al-Tabrisi distinguish throwing stones from shooting arrows. Al-Baghawī reports Muqātil and al-Kalbī's killing by stones; al-Rāzī, al-Nasafī, al-Burūsawī via al-Rāghib, al-Biqāʿī, Asad and Study Quran explicitly connect stones and death. Al-Burūsawī calls it killing in the ugliest manner; al-Biqāʿī adds that Noah's weak followers could not protect him. Ibn ʿĀshūr says rajm means throwing stones and commonly death by stoning. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī takes the threat physically and calls verbal abuse remote; al-Bayḍāwī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān allow both physical and verbal senses. Al-Māwardī cites Abū Dāwūd's poetic tarajmunī as usage evidence without specifying in the note which sense it proves. Al-Rāzī elsewhere explains Satan's designation rajīm through meteors cast at devils from heaven, later extended to evil rebels. Islahi says the earlier threat of stoning was ignored and now will be executed."}, {"id": "26:116/q05/p2", "position": "He would be killed; these glosses do not specify the manner of killing.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Ḥasan, Zayd ibn Aslam, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Kalbī and Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan are cited for killing. Al-Wāḥidī al-Wajīz gives killing as an alternative to insults. Al-Thumālī, cited by al-Thaʿlabī and al-Qurṭubī, says Quranic stoning means killing except at 19:46, where it means insult. Al-Biqāʿī's note says al-mujrimīn means those killed, with Noah's weak followers unable to protect him."}, {"id": "26:116/q05/p3", "position": "He would be verbally abused, insulted or reviled; 'stoning' pictures blame cast at him.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī glosses the threat as reviling; al-Suddī, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and other reports give verbal abuse. Al-Jishumī and al-Tabrisi explain the metaphor as pelting someone with blame; Ibn ʿAṭiyya adds slander, and al-Ālūsī calls it taunting. Al-Wāḥidī al-Wajīz, al-Bayḍāwī and Abū Ḥayyān include it as an alternative sense. Study Quran compares Satan called al-rajīm, usually understood as accursed. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports this figurative view but rejects it as remote. Al-Thumālī's generalization, cited by al-Thaʿlabī and al-Qurṭubī, excludes this verse from the verbal sense by making 19:46 the exception."}, {"id": "26:116/q05/p4", "position": "He would be among people marked by ill omen or misfortune.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī reports this explanation from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, distinct from other sources' reports of al-Ḍaḥḥāk's verbal-abuse gloss."}]}
{"id": "26:116/q06", "question": "What does مِنَ ٱلْمَرْجُومِينَ add to the threat?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:116/q06/p1", "position": "It places Noah in the class of people deemed deserving of that punishment.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr compares the classifying construction with Noah's words وما أنا من المهتدين in 6:56."}]}
{"id": "26:116/q07", "question": "What does ṭard mean in the lexical discussion of ٱلْمَرْجُومِينَ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:116/q07/p1", "position": "Ṭard is expulsion or banishment, driving someone away or making them an outcast.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī equates the verbs ṭaradahu and aṭradahu with driving a person away or making an outcast; the note does not explicitly equate ṭard with this verse's threatened rajm."}]}
{"id": "26:116/q08", "question": "How do other Quranic uses of stoning bear on this threat?", "turns_on": "The analogies differ: Abraham's father's threat in 19:46 is verbal abuse, while Satan's epithet is explained through meteors or as 'accursed'.", "positions": [{"id": "26:116/q08/p1", "position": "The threat in 19:46 means verbal abuse, showing that stoning language can be figurative.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī identifies Abraham's father's words in 19:46 as an insult; Study Quran cites his comparison for a metaphorical reading of stoning here. Al-Thumālī, as quoted by al-Thaʿlabī and al-Qurṭubī, agrees on 19:46 but makes it the sole exception to killing elsewhere in the Quran."}, {"id": "26:116/q08/p2", "position": "The title rajīm for Satan relates to devils driven from heaven by meteors and is extended to evil rebels.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī gives the meteors as an alternative explanation for Satan's title and cites 26:116 and 36:18. Study Quran reports the usual understanding of al-rajīm as 'accursed' when illustrating a figurative sense."}]}
{"id": "26:116/q09", "question": "At what stage of Noah's dealings with his people did the threat come?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:116/q09/p1", "position": "It came near the end of prolonged, failed efforts to call and persuade them, as their opposition hardened.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr says Noah called night and day, openly and privately, while unbelief and resistance increased. Al-Biqāʿī says that after he refused to expel the followers they dropped deceptive inducement and threatened death; Ibn ʿĀshūr says they resorted to physical threats when argument failed. Al-Ālūsī quotes Irshād al-ʿAql al-Salīm that the threat came near the end. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls it the last stage of dealings, al-Rāzī connects it with Noah's despair of their salvation, and Islahi infers an earlier ignored stoning threat."}]}
{"id": "26:116/q10", "question": "What happened to Noah amid his people's hostility?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:116/q10/p1", "position": "They attacked and strangled him until he fainted; after recovering he prayed for their forgiveness.", "reasons": "Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmits ʿAbd ibn ʿUmayr al-Laythī's report of Noah saying, 'Lord, forgive my people, for they do not know.'"}]}
{"id": "26:116/q11", "question": "How does the threat lead into Noah's prayer in 26:117?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:116/q11/p1", "position": "Threatened with death by stoning, Noah despaired of their salvation and asked God to judge between them.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī explicitly joins the threat to the appeal in 26:117."}]}
{"id": "26:116/q12", "question": "How does this narrative fit the sūra's other messenger accounts?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:116/q12/p1", "position": "Noah's call, his people's beliefs and their response parallel those of Moses and Abraham; the narrative groups give the same message.", "reasons": "Kuranyolu compares the essential principles and responses across the three accounts and mentions 11:25 and 11:49."}]}
{"id": "26:124/q01", "question": "How does 'when he said to them' relate to the account of denial?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:124/q01/p1", "position": "It gives the time of ʿĀd's denial: Hūd addressed them as they rejected the messengers.", "reasons": "Bursevī explicitly attaches the temporal clause to the account of denial. Al-Ṭabarī describes ʿĀd as denying God's messengers when their brother Hūd urged them to fear punishment for disbelief."}]}
{"id": "26:124/q02", "question": "Who are the people Hūd addresses, and where did they live?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:124/q02/p1", "position": "They are ʿĀd; a report places them in Yemen at al-Aḥqāf, the sand dunes.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī and Ṭabāṭabāʾī identify Hūd's people as ʿĀd. Al-Suddī, reported by Ibn Abī Ḥātim, locates them in Yemen at al-Aḥqāf and explains the name as sand dunes."}]}
{"id": "26:124/q03", "question": "Why is Hūd called their brother?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:124/q03/p1", "position": "He belonged to their people by lineage and was personally known to them, though he did not share their religion.", "reasons": "Muqātil and al-Baghawī explicitly distinguish lineage from religion; al-Ṭabrisī and Bursevī also state lineage. Al-Biqāʿī says they already knew his sincerity, counsel and fidelity, so they should have reflected before rejecting him. Iṣlāḥī says he was no stranger and his impeccable life made their treatment of him as a liar or fabricator especially unfortunate. Samarrāʾī's comparison explains that Shuʿayb is called Midian's brother because he belonged to Midian, but not the Aykah people's brother; he cites 7:85, 11:84 and 23:36."}]}
{"id": "26:124/q04", "question": "What is reported about Hūd's name and life?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:124/q04/p1", "position": "Some say his original name was ʿĀbir, he was called Hūd for dignity and calmness, lived 150 years, and was sent to ʿĀd at forty.", "reasons": "Bursevī transmits this as the view of 'some'; the reported reason for the name is his dignity and calmness."}]}
{"id": "26:124/q05", "question": "What does Hūd's question call his people to do?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:124/q05/p1", "position": "Fear God and His punishment by ending disobedience, especially associating partners with Him, and worship Him alone.", "reasons": "Muqātil glosses it as fearing God; al-Ṭabarī specifies fear of punishment for disbelief; Elmalılı likewise reads it as asking whether they fear God. Al-Ṭabrisī and Kur'an Yolu explain piety as avoiding disobedience. Bursevī adds stopping their conduct, especiall

y shirk, lest they incur punishment. Al-Biqāʿī says they must fear their Creator, worship Him alone and leave powerless associates that can neither harm nor benefit. Al-Qurṭubī and Ibn ʿĀshūr refer the explanation to the preceding or parallel opening of Noah's story. Iṣlāḥī describes the warning as a remaining chance to abandon wrongdoing and follow the messenger instead of corrupt leaders."}]}
{"id": "26:124/q06", "question": "What tone does the opening 'alā' give Hūd's appeal?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:124/q06/p1", "position": "It is a gentle, earnest and affectionate warning that leaves the people a chance to change course.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says alā makes the exhortation courteous and soft enough to reach them. Iṣlāḥī calls the repeated prophetic appeal an earnest, affectionate final warning: they can still forsake wrongdoing and follow their messenger rather than corrupt leaders."}]}
{"id": "26:124/q07", "question": "How did ʿĀd respond to Hūd's admonition?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:124/q07/p1", "position": "They rejected him and the messengers; a report says they demanded the punishment he warned of.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī states that ʿĀd denied God's messengers when Hūd urged fear of punishment. Al-Suddī, reported by Ibn Abī Ḥātim, says Hūd admonished them and recalled the Qur'anic account, but they denied him and demanded punishment. Al-Biqāʿī stresses that rejection came without pausing to consider their known brother's sincerity. Iṣlāḥī says they treated a man whose impeccable life they knew as a liar or fabricator."}]}
{"id": "26:124/q08", "question": "How does Hūd's address follow the pattern of the other prophets' addresses?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:124/q08/p1", "position": "He addresses his own people with the recurring prophetic call to piety, within the shared pattern of trustworthiness, obedience and seeking no wage.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says Hūd addresses them as other messengers address their peoples. Al-Qurṭubī and Ibn ʿĀshūr explain his call by the preceding or parallel opening of Noah's story. The Study Quran says Hūd's first five verses match Noah's opening and those of later prophets, citing 26:105–109, 141–145, 160–164 and 176–180. Samarrāʾī notes that the other prophets in this sūra address their own peoples, contrasting Shuʿayb's relation to Midian and Aykah; he cites 7:85, 11:84 and 23:36. Some exegetes reported by Ṭabāṭabāʾī say the recurring assertions of prophetic trustworthiness, refusal of wages, and calls to piety and obedience show a shared mission of true knowledge and conduct leading to reward and away from punishment, despite differing detailed laws across eras. Iṣlāḥī describes the recurring appeal as an earnest, affectionate final warning to follow the messenger rather than corrupt leaders."}]}
{"id": "26:124/q09", "question": "Why does the account speak of denying the messengers when ʿĀd rejected Hūd?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:124/q09/p1", "position": "The plural description accompanies their outward rejection of one messenger, as it does in Noah's story.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī observes that the people are called deniers of the messengers even though they outwardly rejected only Hūd; the same pattern occurs in Noah's story. Al-Ṭabarī also describes ʿĀd as denying God's messengers when Hūd warned them, but gives no further explanation here."}]}
{"id": "26:124/q10", "question": "What role does Hūd's story have in this sūra's sequence?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:124/q10/p1", "position": "It helps detail the intervening nations' dealings with their messengers and fates in historical order, each account ending with a refrain.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī compares the previous sūra, which detailed Moses and Noah but briefly mentioned the nations between them, with this sūra's fuller ordered accounts and recurring refrain."}]}
{"id": "26:124/q11", "question": "Where else is the account of Hūd and ʿĀd discussed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:124/q11/p1", "position": "At 7:65, to which Asad directs readers along with its note 48.", "reasons": "Asad gives 7:65 and his note 48 as the cross-reference for the account of Hūd and ʿĀd."}]}
{"id": "26:124/q12", "question": "How do terms for distance differ in related passages?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:124/q12/p1", "position": "Buʿd is the opposite of nearness; naʾy specifically conveys turning away and refusal, the opposite of turning toward.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ contrasts their usage across 11:95, 11:44, 11:60, 11:68, 23:41, 23:44, 2:176, 22:52, 41:52, 14:3, 14:18, 4:6, 4:116, 4:136, 4:167, 22:12, 42:18, 34:8 and 50:27."}]}
{"id": "26:126/q01", "question": "What does fearing God require here?", "turns_on": "The notes variously explain God-fearing through worship, obedience and moral reform, acceptance of the messenger, fear of punishment, the people's particular excesses, or an inward spiritual discipline.", "positions": [{"id": "26:126/q01/p1", "position": "Obey God and turn from disobedience toward praiseworthy conduct.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari specifies following God's commands and prohibitions.
